ai.title_zh: 整合表观遗传学与转录组学识别人类血液中的衰老基因
ai.summary_zh: 该论文提出一种整合表观遗传与转录组年龄相关变化的方法,利用高分辨率多组学数据识别血液中同时具有表观遗传和转录组年龄依赖变化的基因组区域。摘要称这些多组学衰老基因富集适应性免疫功能,在多样人群中复制更稳健,且与衰老相关结局的关联强于单独使用表观遗传或转录组数据识别的基因,并可能作为表观遗传编辑的靶点。提供的证据包含论文元数据、图注(Fig.1–Fig.4)以及作者代码仓库的静态观察记录;作者代码未被执行,静态检查不构成复现验证。
learning_points: 论文主题为整合表观遗传(DNA甲基化)与转录组数据识别人类血液中的衰老基因,发表于 Nature Communications。
Fig.1 展示6个RNA-seq队列(MESA1、MESA2、PPMI、GC6、500FG、JenAge)的年龄分布、前10个年龄相关转录本,以及CD248表达随年龄的负相关(各队列Pearson r 约 -0.34 至 -0.56)。
Fig.2 比较年龄相关DNAm增益区域与基因表达随年龄的相关性,并展示年龄相关下调基因启动子DNAm与年龄的相关性,涉及MESA1、MESA2、PPMI队列。
Fig.3 在MGB队列中展示年龄与衰老CpG处DNAm水平的相关性,并比较不同队列(含RA、Grady、GENOA)的CpG位点样本量。
Fig.4 用火山图和森林图展示DNAm水平与死亡率的关联,采用Cox比例风险回归并按年龄、性别调整,使用Benjamini-Hochberg FDR校正。
作者代码仓库固定提交为54c8c2336be354a8a74a5f87a8d3c120b42ca921,包含R脚本与多个Jupyter notebook;静态观察显示部分notebook无法解析,需人工复核。

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: AROCMs in blood samples from S = 90 dog breeds.Top panels connect AROCMs to a Lifespan, b 1/Lifespan, c adult weight, and d Log(Cor(Age, Methyl)) versus Log(Lifespan); bottom panels tie Adj. AROCM to the same factors (e, f, g), and h Log(Adj.Cor) versus Log(Lifespan). Pearson correlations and corresponding two-sided t-test p-values are reported in each panel. Gray error bands in d, h are 95% confidence bands of the LOESS smooth curve fitted to the data. Both adjusted and unadjusted AROCMs were computed with p = 552 CpGs in bivalent promoter 2 bound by polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) (BivProm2+)57. Each integer label corresponds to a different dog breed (Supplementary Data 1).
figures.attribution: Steve Horvath; Joshua Zhang; Amin Haghani; Ake T. Lu; Zhe Fei. Fundamental equations linking methylation dynamics to maximum lifespan in mammals. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-51855-z. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption: Age versus mean methylation in select chromatin states in mammals.a Displays the Spearman correlation between the inverse of mammalian maximum lifespan 1/L (x-axis) and the AROCM of diverse chromatin states. Each dot represents one of the 54 universal chromatin states57, with the AROCM defined per Methods. Only chromatin states with Spearman correlation exceeding 0.6 or below −0.3 with the inverse of maximum lifespan are labeled. More details are in Supplementary Data 2. The most pronounced correlation is found for CpGs in bivalent promoter 2 also bound by polycomb repressive complex 2 (BivProm2+). b Scaled Mean Methylation versus Relative Age across all samples; c Scaled Mean Methylation against Log-linear Transformed Relative Age in all samples. Black curves mark the overall trend. In panel c, a linear regression line was fitted per species. d–f Depicts AROCM calculation for BivProm2+ state in 3 species-tissue strata. Colored line segments/numbers in each panel represent: Young AROCM for age interval [0, 0.1L) in green; Old AROCM for age interval (0.1L, L) in blue; AROCM for age interval [0, L) in red. Pearson correlations and corresponding two-sided t-test p-values are reported in b–f. The sample size for each panel is reported on the x-axis label. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.
figures.attribution: Steve Horvath; Joshua Zhang; Amin Haghani; Ake T. Lu; Zhe Fei. Fundamental equations linking methylation dynamics to maximum lifespan in mammals. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-51855-z. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.caption: Scaled mean methylation against relative age or log-linear transformed relative age in 6 additional species-tissue strata.The correlations increase and associations become more linear post-transformation. a–c, g–i Scaled Mean Methylation versus Relative Age, the red dashed line represents the linear fit to relative age, the blue dashed curve represents the inverse transformation of the linear fit in (d–f, j–l); d–f, j–l Scaled Mean Methylation versus Log-linear transformed relative age, where γ1 is the AROCM defined in equation (29), with ScaledMi = γ0 + γ1Ti. A two-sided z-test is used to calculate the p-values for γ1. Pearson correlations and corresponding two-sided t-test p-values are reported in each panel. The sample size for each panel is reported on the x-axis label. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.
figures.attribution: Steve Horvath; Joshua Zhang; Amin Haghani; Ake T. Lu; Zhe Fei. Fundamental equations linking methylation dynamics to maximum lifespan in mammals. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-51855-z. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.caption: AROCM in young animals versus that in old animals.a, b, c Natural log-transformed values of AROCM in young animals versus AROCM calculated in old animals. Mean methylation was defined with respect to CpGs located in chromatin state a BivProm2+, b BivProm1+, c ReprPC1+. d, e, f Corresponding plots on the original scale, i.e., without log transformation. Each dot corresponds to a different species. Median aggregation was used to combine AROCM results from different tissues by species. x-axis: AROCM for young samples (Relative Age R < 0.1). y-axis: AROCM for old samples (R > = 0.1). Samples are labeled by mammalian species numbers. Each panel reports the Pearson correlation value Cor and the corresponding two-sided t-test p-value. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

figures.label: Fig. 5
figures.caption: AROCM versus maximum mammalian lifespan excluding outlying species.a Log AROCM versus Log Lifespan; b AROCM against a/Lifespan; c Log Adj.AROCM versus Log Lifespan (equation (20)); d Adj.AROCM against a/Lifespan (equation (25)). Each dot reports a species-level result (median across tissues) with N = 125 species. Pearson correlations and the corresponding two-sided t-test p-values are reported for each panel. Dotted lines in b, d denote x = y. Supplementary Fig. 3 contains results for young and old AROCM. We conducted an analogous analysis on strata with comparable SD (R) values, see Supplementary Fig. 5. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

figures.caption: AROCM versus maximum mammalian lifespan including outlying species.This figure is similar to Figure 5 but it includes the outlying species and strata, i.e., we skipped the filtering approach described in Methods. a–c Each dot reports a species-level result (median across tissues) with N = 133 species. d–f Species-tissue strata analysis based on N = 249 species-tissue strata (represented by the dots). a, d AROCM versus Lifespan; b, e Log AROCM versus Log Lifespan; c, f AROCM against 1/Lifespan; Pearson correlations and the corresponding two-sided t-test p-values are reported for each panel. figures.label: Fig. 7
figures.caption: Lifespan group analysis of age correlations.Cor(Methyl, Age) and Adj.Cor versus groups of species by maximum lifespan. a, b Non-significant associations between Cor(Methyl, RelAge) and lifespan groups. c, d Adjusted Cor (equation (18)) by Lifespan groups. e, f Log of Cor(Methyl,Age) and Adj.Cor versus Log of Lifespan. p-values are based on the Mann-Kendall Trend Test. These results illustrate condition (C1) in Methods. For each box, the dots correspond to individual strata, the center line is the median; the box limits are upper and lower quartiles; the whiskers are 1.5 times the interquartile range. Data were obtained by analyzing WGBS datasets from human CD4+ T-cells (6 samples 18–86 years old, GSE79798 and 2 samples 0 and 103 years old, GSE31263), human epidermis (12 samples from 6 different ages, each age including a sun-exposed and sun-protected sample averaged for this analysis, GSE52972), and mouse hepatocytes (8 samples, 4 2 months vs 4 22 months, GSE89274). PRC2 binding was evaluated using EZH2 and SUZ12 ChIP-Seq data from ENCODE in H1 hESCs and in mESCs (see Supplementary Data 1). One outlier sample was removed (see “Methods” section). b Average DNAm levels at high-PRC2 LMRs shown for each autosomal chromosome. c Average DNAm levels at high-PRC2 LMRs in skin-exposed versus skin-protected samples derived from donors of different ages. Each sample of the same age (skin protected and skin exposed) derives from the same donor. Data are from the same human epidermis WGBS datasets shown in a. High-PRC2 LMRs (top 1000 PRC2-binding LMRs in a given tissue) are highlighted with dotted red boxes.

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.caption: Gain of DNAm at PRC2 targets is measurable using different assays.a Average DNAm levels at CpGs across the whole genome (left panel) and at low-methylated CpGs (LMCs) ranked by the level of their PRC2 binding in hESCs (right panels). Data were obtained by analyzing DNA methylation microarray data from human PBMC samples. Data from four different HM450 datasets (GSE40279, n = 656, GSE42861, n = 689, GSE152027, n = 471, and GSE55763, n = 2711) are shown in each panel. PRC2 binding was estimated by using EZH2 and SUZ12 ChIP-Seq data from ENCODE in the H1 cell line (see “Methods” section). b Average DNAm levels in different mouse tissues at LMCs ranked by the level of their PRC2 binding in mESCs (left panel). The right panel shows the same data represented as averages. Data were obtained from an RRBS dataset (GSE120137). One outlier sample was removed from all analyses (see “Methods” section). One-sided independent t-tests were performed between young and old for each tissue (adipose p = 1.4e−09, blood p = 2.2e−04, kidney p = 7.6e−03, liver p = 1.5e−16, lung p = 1.1e−09, muscle p = 4.9e−04). c Average DNAm levels at LMCs with high-PRC2 binding in mESCs, in mouse hepatocytes from scWGBS dataset (SRP069120). One outlier sample was removed from each category according to Trapp et al.74 (see “Methods” section). One-sided independent t-tests were performed between young and old samples (p = 4.9e−04). p-value cutoffs for all boxplots are represented graphically by *<0.05, **<0.01, ***<0.001, ****<0.0001. For boxplots, boxes show the quartiles of the dataset with median bar in the center of the box, whiskers represent the range of data (excluding any outliers which are represented as black circles).

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: Single-cell and single-nucleus skeletal muscle aging atlas.a, Visual overview of experimental design and main directions of investigations. Illustration was created with BioRender.com. b, Timescale displaying human muscle sampling across ages for scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq (eight young versus nine aged) and for myofiber subtyping (seven young versus four aged). c, Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) visualization of annotated cells in the Muscle Aging Cell Atlas. Cell type annotation and abbreviations for all populations are shown in Supplementary Table 10. d, log2-transformed fold change (FC) in the abundance of cell clusters across age (first column) and enrichment in cells compared to nuclei fraction (second and third columns), taking into account 10x chemistry (see full version in Extended Data Fig. 1d). Some populations (hybrid, specialized myonuclei, MF-Isn fragments, MF-IIsn fragments, neutrophils, mesothelium, red blood cells (RBC), eosinophils and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC)) were removed from the plot because they represented a mixture of different cell types, contained a very small number of cells or predominantly originated from particular donors. The LTSR denotes statistical significance and ranges from 0 to 1, where 1 indicates a confident estimate. See Methods for more details. ArtEC, arterial endothelial cells; CapEC, capillary endothelial cells; cDC1 and cDC2, conventional type 1 and 2 dendritic cells; mSchwann and nmSchwann, myelinating and non-myelinating Schwann cells.Source data

ai.title_zh: 人类骨骼肌衰老图谱(Human skeletal muscle aging atlas)
ai.summary_zh: 该资料为发表于 Nature Aging(2024-04-15,DOI:10.1038/s43587-024-00613-3)的论文条目,摘要称对成人肋间肌进行单细胞与单核转录组分析(90,902 个单细胞与 92,259 个单核,来自 17 位供体),刻画各肌肉区室的衰老变化,并给出在线资源与配套小鼠肌肉图谱。提供的证据包含 Fig. 1–Fig. 4 的图注文本、若干 DE_analysis 脚本的静态观察片段,以及一条关于 Notebook 文件名与 Fig. 1d 对应关系的注释。作者代码未被执行,因此本条目仅作待核学习注释,不构成复现验证。
learning_points: 论文主题为人类骨骼肌衰老图谱,期刊为 Nature Aging,时间为 2024-04-15(evidence: publication)。
摘要称研究覆盖 90,902 个单细胞与 92,259 个单核、17 位供体,取材为成人肋间肌,并给出在线资源与配套小鼠肌肉图谱(evidence: publication)。
Fig. 1 展示实验设计与研究方向的视觉概览、跨年龄采样时间轴(scRNA-seq/snRNA-seq 为 8 年轻 vs 9 年老;肌纤维分型为 7 年轻 vs 4 年老)、UMAP 注释可视化,以及细胞簇丰度随年龄的 log2 倍数变化与细胞/细胞核富集比较(evidence: figure-0)。
Fig. 2 聚焦人 MuSC 衰老机制,包含 MuSC 亚群 UMAP、GO 词条树、Milo 蜂群图、核糖体生物发生富集评分(5 年轻 vs 7 年老,双尾 Mann–Whitney–Wilcoxon 检验)、核糖体生物发生与 RNA 聚合酶 I 复合体基因点图,以及衰老相关与核糖体组装基因表达(evidence: figure-1)。
Fig. 3 为整合的单细胞与单核肌纤维图谱,含整合/分别的 UMAP、剪接与未剪接转录本比例饼图、肌核群体 Milo 蜂群图(注明供体 343B 因 II-OTU 状态比例异常被剔除)、FAM189A2+ 与 OTUD1+ 状态的标记基因谱与 RNAscope 染色、NMJ 及辅助标记基因点图与 RNAscope 染色(evidence: figure-2)。
Fig. 4 关注对抗衰老中快肌纤维丢失的机制,含肌纤维类别与对应肌核示意图、免疫荧光染色与比例变化(7 年轻 vs 4 年老)、基于 MYH1/MYH2/MYH7 的三维肌核散点图与比例变化(5 年轻 vs 5 年老,剔除 3 位未分类比例 >75% 的供体)、RNAscope 联合免疫荧光,以及快肌结构基因小提琴图(evidence: figure-3)。
DE_analysis 下四个 run.R 脚本(human scell coarse/granular、human snuclei coarse/granular)的静态观察显示读取 features.csv 与 metadata.csv、以 Y.Rbin 为转置表达矩阵,但脚本未被执行(evidence: script-0、script-1、script-2、script-3)。
有一条注释称 Notebook 文件名直接标记 Fig1d,图注说明细胞组成 fold change 与 LTSR,与 Notebook 的 CellTypeCompositionAnalysis 和点图函数一致(evidence: curated-note)。

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: Cell-type-specific transcriptomic aging clocks for neurogenic regions.a, Training data for single-cell transcriptomic aging clocks. 10x Genomics single-cell transcriptomics on SVZ neurogenic regions from four independent cohorts of 4–8 male mice, aged 3.3 to 29 months (Supplementary Table 1). SVZ regions from the same cohort were multiplexed using LMO labeling (MULTI-seq). b, UMAP projection of 21,458 high-quality cells from SVZ single-cell transcriptomes across cohorts. Each dot represents the transcriptome of an individual cell with transcripts detected from at least 500 genes. c, Same as in b but colored by mouse age. Two pairs of mice had the same age, resulting in 26 age colors (28 mice). d, Same as in b but colored by the predicted cell cycle state based on Seurat’s CellCycleScoring function. e, Schematic depicting the generation of BootstrapCells for training chronological clocks. From each cell type and sample, 15 cells were sampled and combined to generate one BootstrapCell. This process was repeated 100 times per cell type and sample combination, to generate a training dataset that equally weighted each SVZ sample. f, SVZ proliferative fraction (cells predicted to be G2/M or S phase) as a function of chronological age. R represents Pearson’s correlation coefficient. The gray band corresponds to the 95% confidence interval. g, Schematic depicting the process of generating BootstrapCells for training biological age clocks. Biological age was defined as the SVZ proliferative fraction (f). h, Predicted biological age as a function of predicted chronological age. R represents Pearson’s correlation coefficient. Gray band corresponds to 95% confidence interval. i, Performance of BootstrapCell chronological age prediction across cell types. Density of BootstrapCell predictions is depicted in color and overlaid black dots represent the median prediction for each sample. Performance is based on cross-cohort validation. R values are Pearson’s correlation coefficients at the sample level. j, As in i but for BootstrapCell biological age score prediction across cell types. Biological age score is a linear transformation of the SVZ proliferative fraction. k, Overview of Pearson’s correlation coefficients and median absolute error (MAE) values for various methods of predicting chronological age across cell types. SingleCell uses bona fide single-cell transcriptomes with minimal processing as input to a lasso regression model. BootstrapCell uses the preprocessing method depicted in e and a lasso model. EnsembleCell involves repeatedly partitioning cells into groups of 15 cells and training an ensemble of elastic net models. Pseudobulk involves naïve pseudobulking all cells from the same cell type and sample and using a lasso regression model. Performance is based on cross-cohort validation. l, As in k but evaluating biological age prediction.

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption: Generalization of aging clocks to independent datasets and other neurogenic regions.a, External validation of BootstrapCell chronological age prediction models (chronological aging clocks) on single-cell transcriptomic data from young (blue) and old (orange) SVZ samples by Dulken et al.48. Density plots show separated age prediction distributions, indicating ability to discriminate age. b, As in a but evaluating biological age prediction models (biological aging clocks). c, Density plots to assess the generalizability of chronological aging clocks (BootstrapCell) to another mouse neurogenic region using a dataset from Harris et al.60. Transcriptomes of analogous cell types were collected from the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus (another neurogenic region) instead of the SVZ in mice of different ages. There were no microglia in the dataset at the 1-month time point. d, Density plots to assess the generalizability of biological aging clocks (BootstrapCell) to another mouse neurogenic region using a dataset from Harris et al.60 as in c.

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.caption: Genes underlying the cell-type-specific chronological aging clocks.a, Contribution of individual genes to the aNSC-NPC chronological aging clock (BootstrapCell). Donut plots, with sector size denoting gene weight in the model and color indicating sign of expression change with age. Total number of genes used by the clock is in the center. Positive coefficients (orange) indicate increased gene expression in older age. Negative coefficients (blue) indicate decreased gene expression in older age. For other chronological and biological aging clocks, see Extended Data Fig. 2a,b. All genes and coefficients are in Supplementary Table 3. b, UpSet plot illustrating the intersection of gene sets used by cell-type-specific chronological aging clocks. Genes present in four, five or six of the analyzed clocks are highlighted in green, yellow or red, respectively. For biological aging clocks, see Extended Data Fig. 2c. c, Bar plot comparing the impact and count of shared and specific genes within the aNSC-NPC chronological aging clock. Impact is the sum of the absolute value of the gene coefficients. Count is the number of genes in each category. For other chronological and biological aging clocks, see Extended Data Fig. 2d,e. d, Expression trajectories as a function of age of select clock-specific genes. Expression values are log-normalized counts per 10,000 transcripts. Bands correspond to 95% confidence intervals. e, Expression trajectories as a function of age of select shared genes across at least four cell-type-specific clocks. Bands correspond to 95% confidence intervals. f, Top enriched Gene Ontology (GO) biological process terms from GSEA of genes selected by chronological aging clocks. g, Assessment of the ability of cell-type-specific clocks to predict age given transcriptomes of different cell types. Size of dots corresponds to Pearson correlation with chronological age and color indicates MAE. Error substantially increases when testing on alternate cell types. For GO term analysis of cell-specific biological aging clocks, see Extended Data Fig. 2f.

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.caption: Effect of heterochronic parabiosis on cell-type-specific aging clocks.a, Schematic of parabiosis cohorts and corresponding UMAP projections from each cohort. Parabiosis cohort 1 dataset was generated with young (5 months) and old (26 months) male mice (number of mice indicated in parentheses); 11,771 high-quality transcriptomes were collected, using one SVZ sample per 10x lane. Parabiosis cohort 2 was generated with young (5 months) and old (21 months) male mice; 13,824 high-quality transcriptomes were collected, using LMOs to multiplex SVZ samples across three 10x lanes. UMAP projection and cell type clustering of SVZ single-cell transcriptomes in cohorts 1 and 2. Each dot represents the transcriptome of an individual cell. Colored by age and intervention (heterochronic parabiosis). For coloration by cell type, see Extended Data Fig. 6a. b, Density plots of the predicted chronological ages for aNSC-NPCs from cohort 1 and cohort 2. Green arrows illustrate the median shift in predicted age between old aNSC-NPCs exposed to young blood (old heterochronic) and old aNSC-NPCs exposed to old blood (old isochronic, control). Density plots for individual mice, and their cohorts of origin, are provided on the right. c, Summary of heterochronic parabiosis effects on chronological age scores across cell types. Effect sizes were calculated by taking the difference in median predicted ages between conditions. Blue color indicates a decrease in predicted chronological age (‘rejuvenation’). Red color indicates an increase in predicted chronological age (‘detrimental impact’). d, Density plots of the predicted biological age scores for neuroblasts from cohort 1 and cohort 2. Green arrows illustrate the median shift in predicted age between old neuroblasts exposed to young circulation (old heterochronic) compared to old neuroblasts exposed to old circulation (old isochronic, control). Density plots for individual mice, and their cohort of origin, are provided on the right. e, Summary of heterochronic parabiosis effects on biological age scores across cell types. Effect sizes are calculated by taking the difference in median predicted ages between conditions. Blue indicates a decrease in predicted chronological age (‘rejuvenation’). Red indicates an increase in predicted biological age. For statistical analysis at the mouse level, see Extended Data Fig. 7a.

figures.label: Fig. 5
figures.caption: Effect of exercise on cell-type-specific aging clocks.a, Schematic of voluntary wheel running experiment and UMAP projection of single-cell transcriptomes. For the exercise cohort, 4 young (4.5 months) or 3–4 old (21.5 months) male mice were transferred into cages with either a freely spinning wheel or no wheel. Wheel rotations were tracked to verify that mice indeed exercised. After 5 weeks, SVZ niches were collected, so mice were ~6 months and 23 months at time of collection, and 15 lanes of 10x Genomics transcriptomics performed without sample multiplexing. UMAP projection and cell-type clustering of SVZ single-cell transcriptomes in the exercise cohort. Each dot represents the transcriptome of an individual cell. Colored by age and intervention (exercise) or by cell type (UMAP; Extended Data Fig. 8a). b, Density plots of predicted chronological ages of oligodendrocytes by age and exercise condition. Exercise consistently rejuvenated oligodendrocyte transcriptomes regardless of age. c, Summary of exercise effects on chronological age scores across cell types and ages. Effect sizes were calculated by taking the difference in median predicted ages between conditions. Blue indicates a decrease in predicted chronological age (‘rejuvenation’). Red indicates an increase in predicted chronological age (‘detrimental impact’). d, Density plots of aNSC-NPC predicted biological ages. Exercise rejuvenated aNSC-NPC transcriptomes of both young and old mice. e, Summary of exercise effects on biological age scores across cell types and ages. Effect sizes were calculated by taking the difference in median predicted ages between conditions. Blue indicates a decrease in predicted biological age (‘rejuvenation’). Red indicates an increase in predicted chronological age (‘detrimental impact’). For statistical analysis at the mouse level, see Extended Data Fig. 7b.

figures.label: Fig. 6
figures.caption: Comparison of exercise and parabiosis interventions on cell-type-specific aging clocks.a, Bar plot comparing effects of different interventions. Bar represents the difference (in months) between predicted chronological ages between controls and intervention. Parabiosis cohorts 1 and 2 were averaged. b, Pie charts of the directional effect and overlap of intervention impact on aNSC-NPC chronological aging clock genes (BootstrapCell). Genes are called ‘reversed’ when the sign of the log fold change of gene expression in intervention versus control is opposite to the sign of the coefficient of the gene in the clock (indicated on top of the pie charts). Top GO biological process terms and representative genes are listed underneath. c, Venn diagram representing the overlap of DEGs in aNSC-NPCs between young and old mice (‘age’), old heterochronic mice and old isochronic mice (‘young blood’) and old exercised and old sedentary mice (‘exercise’). Differential expression thresholds required a minimum 1.1-fold expression change with a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.1. For aging, mice were grouped as either young (<7 months) or old (>20 months). DEGs shared between age and young blood were interferon-stimulated genes. DEGs shared between age and exercise were genes involved in proliferation, metabolism and development. d, Violin and box plots of gene signatures (sum of normalized gene expression for all genes in the gene set) for ‘interferon-γ response’ and ‘negative regulation of neurogenesis’ for aNSC-NPCs in the parabiosis cohort 1 and cohort 2 combined. In the box plot, the line represents the median and the box represents the interquartile range. P values were obtained from the two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (n = 668, 149 and 146 cells for ‘young isochronic’, ‘old isochronic’ and ‘old heterochronic’, respectively). e, As in d but for aNSC-NPCs in the exercise cohort (n = 2,243, 503 and 1,170 cells for ‘young sedentary’, ‘old sedentary’ and ‘old exercise’, respectively).

figures.label: Fig. 7
figures.caption: Predicting ‘rejuvenation intervention or control’ state on the transcriptomes from mice of different ages to assess intervention relevance to aging.a, Schematic describing how to predict ‘rejuvenation intervention or control’ state on the transcriptomes from mice of different ages to assess intervention relevance to aging. b, Classification results based on logistic regression for the parabiosis intervention in aNSC-NPCs. Correlation between classification results, plotted as (log(p(control) / p(intervention))) and the actual chronological age of aNSC-NPC BootstrapCell transcriptomes. Old mice were more likely to be classified as ‘isochronic old control’, whereas young mice were more likely to be classified as ‘heterochronic old’, indicating that the gene signature that distinguishes exposure to young and old blood is relevant to aging. R is the Pearson correlation. Higher correlation indicates that the main intervention signature overlaps with and reverses age-related changes. c, Summary of correlations between intervention state prediction and chronological age across cell types and interventions, with a separate classifier built for each. The exercise classifiers were built to distinguish old sedentary from old exercised transcriptomes for each cell type. The lower correlation between intervention state predictions and age for the exercise samples implies that the signatures that distinguish exercised and sedentary mice are less related to aging than those derived from parabiosis intervention classifiers.

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 1
figures.caption: Characteristics of the SVZ single-cell transcriptomic data and generalization performance of cell-type-specific aging clocks to humans and generalization of the framework to other cell types and tissues.a, Lipid-modified oligonucleotide cell barcodes detected from 8 SVZ samples multiplexed in one 10x lane. b, Same as in (a) but visualized using tSNE. Samples 5 and 6 were from mice of the same age (and colored in the same color in Fig. 1c). c, Heatmap of single cell gene expression for top 5 cell type markers used for annotation of cell type clusters. Colored bar on top indicates the various cell type clusters. d, Overview of Pearson correlation coefficients (R) and median absolute error (MAE) values for tested methods of predicting chronological age across cell types from single-cell transcriptomic data, including both full distribution (Full) and median metrics only (Median). Performance is based on cross-cohort-validation. e, Correlation plot to assess the generalizability of chronological aging clocks (BoostrapCell) to a human dataset from Hodge et al61. the single-nucleus RNA-seq dataset of the middle temporal gyrus of human patients of different ages (Hodge et al.61). Density of BootstrapCell predictions is depicted in color and overlaid black dots represent the median prediction for each sample. R values are Pearson’s correlation coefficients at the sample level. Bands correspond to 95% confidence interval. f, Performance of chronological aging clocks (BootstrapCell) derived from the single cell RNA-seq multi-tissue atlas Tabula Muris Senis, 2020. Predicted chronological age of endothelial cells from limb muscle, mature natural killer (NK) T cells from spleen, and podocyte cells from kidney from aging clocks built on Tabula Muris Senis as a function of actual chronological age for several mice of different ages. Density of BootstrapCell predictions is depicted in color and overlaid black dots represent the median prediction for each sample. Performance is based on cross-mouse validation. R values are Pearson’s correlation coefficients at the sample level.

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 2
figures.caption: Genes that contribute to the chronological aging clocks and biological aging clocks.a, Contribution of individual genes to the chronological aging clocks (BootstrapCell) (see Fig. 3a for aNSC-NPCs). Donut plots, with sector size denoting gene weight in the model and color indicating sign of expression change with age. Total number of genes used by the clock is provided in the center of each donut plot. Positive coefficients (orange) indicate increased gene expression is associated with older age. Negative coefficients (blue) indicate decreased gene expression is associated with older age. b, As in (a) but for biological aging clocks (BootstrapCell) and their coefficients. c, Upset plot illustrating the intersection of gene sets used by cell-type-specific biological aging clocks. No genes were used in all 6 biological aging clocks. d, Count and coefficient impact of shared and cell-type-specific clock genes for chronological aging clocks. Shared is defined as present in at least one of the other five clocks (see Fig. 3c for aNSC-NPCs). e, As in (d) but for biological aging clocks. f, Top enriched Gene Ontology Biological Process terms from gene set enrichment analysis of genes used in biological aging clocks. Shared genes (present in two or more clocks) are enriched for cytokine-mediated signaling pathway and cellular response to type I interferon. The aNSC-NPC biological aging clock genes are enriched for cell cycle pathways.

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 5
figures.caption: Gene detection rate in cell-type-specific aging clocks.a, Unique genes detected in single cell transcriptomes from the subventricular zone as a function of gene detection rate. Red dots indicate unique genes detected at 2%, 20%, and 80% detection rates. b, Upset plots showing transcriptome overlaps between cell types at different levels of expression detection. Most genes are shared if a very low threshold of detection is used. Above 80% detection rate, transcriptomes are very cell type specific. However, the shared core of easily detected genes in transcriptomes (70 genes) is much larger than the shared core of genes selected by clocks (~1).

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 9
figures.caption: Comparison of genes in cell-type-specific aging clocks impacted by heterochronic parabiosis and by exercise.a, Dot plot summarizing and comparing intervention effects across cell types. Effect sizes for parabiosis were determined by averaging cohort 1 and cohort 2. Exposure to young blood via heterochronic parabiosis has a stronger rejuvenation effect than exercise, and the impact is strongest in aNSC-NPCs. b, Pie charts indicating the overlap and directional effects of different interventions on genes selected by chronological aging clocks (BootstrapCell). Top: selected clock genes increase with age: Bottom: selected clock genes decrease with age. c, Barplots showing the proportion of genes that are differentially expressed age which are reversed by intervention, cell type, and whether the genes increase or decrease with age (abs(ln(fold change)) > 0.1, or approximately greater than a 1.1 fold change with age, FDR < 0.1). Parabiosis is effective at shifting differentially expressed genes during aging towards a more young-associated expression levels (more green in ‘Parabiosis’ column). Reduction of expression of genes that increase with age is larger than the induction of expression of genes that decrease with age (more green in ‘Age Increased’ rows).

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overview of scXMatch. (a) Required inputs: N single-cell profiles xi, binary condition labels yi (orange/purple), a dissimilarity measure d, and the k parameter for k-NN mode. (b–c) A weighted graph G (complete or k-NN) is constructed, and a minimum-weight matching M is computed. (d) The number of cross-matches between conditions yields a P-value to assess global distribution shifts. (e–h) Examples using synthetic data sampled from bivariate normal distributions show that scXMatch detects significant shifts when distributions differ in mean (f, g) or variance (h), but not when they are identical (e).
figures.attribution: Anna Möller; Miriam Schnitzerlein; Eric Greto; Vasily Zaburdaev; Stefan Uderhardt; David B Blumenthal. Quantifying distribution shifts in single-cell data with scXMatch. . DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag706. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.
figures.resolutionStatus: Original PMC cloud source dimensions; maximum publisher resolution not verified

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Results of the scalability tests. (a) Peak memory usage as a function of the number of edges |E| in scXMatch’s k-NN graph. (b–d) Peak memory usage (b), runtime (c), and relative coverage (d) as a function of k, for datasets with different numbers of samples N. Line plots and shaded areas in (b–d) depict means and 95% confidence intervals obtained for datasets with fixed N and k and varying dimensionality h∈{10,500,1000,2000}.
figures.attribution: Anna Möller; Miriam Schnitzerlein; Eric Greto; Vasily Zaburdaev; Stefan Uderhardt; David B Blumenthal. Quantifying distribution shifts in single-cell data with scXMatch. . DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag706. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Benchmarking results on scRNA-seq data. (a) We used ten public scRNA-seq datasets from cells that were subject to perturbations of increasing strengths. (b) P-values obtained with the E-distance test (x-axes, results are identical for all four tested configurations) and scXMatch (y-axes) when comparing control against perturbed cell populations on the ten datasets (columns). Downwards arrows indicate alignment of P-values with perturbation strength. (c) Direct comparison of the relative coverages, required RAM, and runtimes of scXMatch and the E-distance test run in the default configuration suggested by the authors. (d–g) For comparison of our tool scXMatch against commonly used approaches that assess distribution shifts in scRNA-seq data we defined three metrics. (d) MI: Comparing cell populations with increasing perturbation strength against an unperturbed reference population should lead to increasing scores. (e) SSNR: Comparing a perturbed population against the reference should lead to a higher score than comparing disjoint subsets of the perturbed population against each other. (f) SR: Comparing different subsets of the reference against different subsets of the same perturbed condition should lead to similar scores as the comparison of the full data. (g) Benchmarking results of the nine approaches on all ten datasets. For eight of the datasets, scXMatch’s P-value is Pareto-optimal with regard to the three metrics (left panel).
figures.attribution: Anna Möller; Miriam Schnitzerlein; Eric Greto; Vasily Zaburdaev; Stefan Uderhardt; David B Blumenthal. Quantifying distribution shifts in single-cell data with scXMatch. . DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag706. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.
figures.resolutionStatus: Original PMC cloud source dimensions; maximum publisher resolution not verified

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Local outlier factors, colored by inclusion in the MWMCMs obtained for the Norman dataset when using scXMatch with k∈{10,50,100} to compare perturbed cell populations to controls. Plots are annotated with P-values of the Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.
figures.attribution: Anna Möller; Miriam Schnitzerlein; Eric Greto; Vasily Zaburdaev; Stefan Uderhardt; David B Blumenthal. Quantifying distribution shifts in single-cell data with scXMatch. . DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag706. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Importance of dynamic imaging data for distinguishing RTM populations. (a) Snapshot of an unperturbed, sampling macrophage in vivo from the study by Schnitzerlein et al. (2025). Several morphological single-cell features (as schematically drawn on the image) were extracted. They characterize three categories of properties: static morphology, dynamic activity, or adaptation capabilities. While the static features can be calculated from a single image, the latter two require time-lapse images. (b) Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P-values returned by scXMatch (left panel) and the E-distance test (right panel) for pairwise comparisons of RTM populations under different stimuli. Lower left triangle: adjusted P-values Padjall obtained when using all features. Upper right triangle: adjusted P-values Padjstatic obtained when using static features only. The heatmaps are colored according to the difference of these two values (lower triangle minus upper triangle). Strong colors indicate large differences. Since the RTM dataset is small, we could run scXMatch in full graph mode. The standardized Euclidean distance was used as a distance measure. (c) UMAPs of the control versus MCSF-treated RTMs calculated on all and on only the static features, respectively.
figures.attribution: Anna Möller; Miriam Schnitzerlein; Eric Greto; Vasily Zaburdaev; Stefan Uderhardt; David B Blumenthal. Quantifying distribution shifts in single-cell data with scXMatch. . DOI: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btag706. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Fig. 1.
figures.caption: DeCoRE retrieves accurate structural information using enhanced structural profile.(A) Schematic overview of DeCoRE for extracting structural information from nanopore sequencing data. In structure probing experiments, RNA was treated with structure probing chemicals (e.g., NAI-N3) or control reagent (DMSO) and sequenced using nanopore DRS. Then, DeCoRE aligned the reads together with their raw current signals to the reference RNA. For each nucleotide along the reference, a three-feature one-class SVM model was used to identify current signal anomalies in the chemical treated reads by comparing the matched bases, which were subsequently designated as modified bases. The resulting enhanced structural profile of the chemical-treated reads integrates both miscalled bases and modified bases. (B) Performance evaluation of structural profile incorporating both miscalled bases and modified bases in 150 mM Aclm-treated RNA. ROC curves analysis demonstrates strong agreement with known structural models of pri-miR-17∼92a RNA. Using only miscalled bases in Aclm-treated RNA yielded reasonably high agreement with the structural models. (C) ROC curves of reactivity scores calculated by DeCoRE and other methods (Materials and Methods), evaluated on known structural models of pri-miR-17∼92a RNA. (D) The six known structures of pri-miR-17∼92a RNA colored with the reactivity scores calculated by DeCoRE.

DeCoRE: A computational method to resolve RNA structural heterogeneity from RNA structure probing data by direct RNA sequencing.. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aef0670. Copyright holder: The Authors. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.
figures.resolutionStatus: Original PMC cloud source dimensions; maximum publisher resolution not verified

figures.label: Fig. 2.
figures.caption: DeCoRE identifies the known heterogenous structures of riboswitches.(A) Schematic of the clustering approach used to resolve heterogenous structures from enhanced structural profiles. Each read’s structural profile was encoded as a vector, where bases were categorized as 0 (matched bases, blue), 1 (modified bases, light blue), or 2 (miscalled bases, red). All vectors were padding to the same length (L) corresponding to the reference RNA. (B) Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) of the vectorized structural profile of each read in chemical-treated sample of the lysine riboswitch, colored by the cluster identified by DeCoRE. The silhouette score (si) was used to assess the clustering quality. The relative proportions of each cluster were indicated. (C) Barplots displayed the reactivity scores of the two structural cluster identified by DeCoRE in the region harboring the two mutually exclusive conformations of the lysine riboswitch—the antiterminator and transcription terminator states. The three key regions distinguishing the two conformations are highlighted by gray boxes and blue lines, and the base-pairing patterns in these regions for the two conformations was indicated by dashed lines. (D) The two structural models corresponding to the antiterminator and transcription terminator states were colored with the DeCoRE’s cluster-specific reactivity scores. (E) UMAP of the vectorized structural profile of each read in chemical-treated sample of the TPP riboswitch, colored by the cluster identified by DeCoRE. The relative proportions of each cluster were indicated. (F) The structure model of TPP riboswitch aptamer region (THI element) under ON and OFF state (24), colored with the DeCoRE’s cluster-specific reactivity scores. In the TPP-bound OFF state, J4/5 and J2/3 stack onto the TPP ligand, and loop L5 rearranges to form hydrogen bonds with P3, in contrast to the ON state.
figures.attribution: Yong Huang; Jinsong Zhang; Lei Sun; Qiangfeng Cliff Zhang. DeCoRE: A computational method to resolve RNA structural heterogeneity from RNA structure probing data by direct RNA sequencing.. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aef0670. Copyright holder: The Authors. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.
figures.resolutionStatus: Original PMC cloud source dimensions; maximum publisher resolution not verified

figures.label: Fig. 3.
figures.caption: DeCoRE reveals structural transitions during B. subtilis 16S rRNA transcription.(A) Schematic overview of the experimental workflow used to generate the transcriptional intermediates of B. subtilis 16S rRNA in vitro and detect their structures using nanopore DRS–based structure probing method. (B) PCC of reactivity scores between each intermediate and the full-length 16S rRNA within their shared nucleotide regions. (C) Left heatmap showed the reactivity scores of 136 intermediates, categorized on the basis of their 3′ end alignment positions with 10-nt resolution. Each row represents the reactivity scores of a specific intermediate with length indicated by the y axis. Each column represents the reactivity score trajectories for a specific nucleotide, indicated along the x axis. Nucleotides highlighted with asterisk were examples [analyzed in (D)], which exhibit substantial reactivity score variation across different intermediates. Right line plot showed the read count distribution of each transcriptional intermediate. (D) Reactivity trajectories of three representative residues, corresponding to the highlighted nucleotides in (B), illustrate distinct structural transition patterns: G162 exhibits early base-pairing (“immediate pairing”), C192 remains unpaired across intermediates (“immediate unpaired”), and G178 shows mixed reactivity indicative of dynamic structural shifts. (E) Reactivity score profiles and predicted structure models of the selected intermediates of lengths 200 to 210 nt (L200_210), 300 to 310 nt (L300_310), and 600 to 610 nt (L600_610). The structure model of each intermediate was predicted using their all nucleotides with the reactivity scores as constraints.
figures.attribution: Yong Huang; Jinsong Zhang; Lei Sun; Qiangfeng Cliff Zhang. DeCoRE: A computational method to resolve RNA structural heterogeneity from RNA structure probing data by direct RNA sequencing.. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aef0670. Copyright holder: The Authors. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Fig. 4.
figures.caption: DeCoRE uncovers structural heterogeneity and dynamic folding of B. subtilis 16S rRNA during the transcription.(A) UMAP of the vectorized structural profile of each read in chemical-treated sample of the five 16S rRNA transcriptional intermediates with high coverage, colored by the cluster identified by DeCoRE. The relative proportions of each cluster were indicated. (B) Scatter plot of the PCA analysis of reactivity scores for the 1- to 270-nt, 1- to 320-nt, and 1- to 670-nt regions of each conformation across all five intermediates. Each dot represents a conformation that predicted within the corresponding region, labeled with structural model free energy (kcal/mol). Dot colors indicate conformation category, and dots belonging to the same structurally related group are connected by dashed lines. Dot size reflects the relative abundance of each conformation within the corresponding transcription intermediates. (C) PCC of reactivity scores between the two conformations for each of the three intermediates: L270_280, L320_330, and L670_680, calculated using a 50-nt sliding window.

ai.title_zh: DeCoRE:利用直接RNA测序的结构探测数据解析RNA结构异质性的计算方法
ai.summary_zh: 该资料介绍了一种名为DeCoRE(deconvolving complex RNA structural ensembles)的计算方法,旨在利用直接RNA测序(direct RNA sequencing)在单个转录本水平上解析RNA结构异质性与动态变化。摘要称DeCoRE结合增强的结构信号检测与测序读段直接聚类,可在单核苷酸分辨率下解析RNA结构集合,并展示其在赖氨酸与TPP核糖开关已知替代构象以及细菌核糖体RNA共转录折叠路径上的应用。所提供的证据包含四张图的图注(涉及方法流程、核糖开关聚类、16S rRNA转录中间体结构转变与异质性)以及若干脚本的静态观察记录。作者代码未执行,输入尺度与图号对应关系未明示处保持未知,AI注释仅为待核学习材料。
learning_points: DeCoRE被描述为一种面向直接RNA测序结构探测数据的计算方法,目标是在单个转录本水平解析RNA结构异质性与动态(evidence: publication)。
Fig. 1图注描述了DeCoRE从纳米孔测序数据提取结构信息的流程:RNA经结构探测化学试剂(如NAI-N3)或对照试剂(DMSO)处理,经纳米孔DRS测序后,将读段及其原始电流信号比对到参考RNA,并对每个核苷酸使用三特征one-class SVM模型识别化学处理读段中的电流信号异常(evidence: figure-0)。
Fig. 1图注提到增强结构谱整合了误判碱基(miscalled bases)与修饰碱基(modified bases),并在150 mM Aclm处理的RNA中评估性能,ROC曲线分析显示与pri-miR-17∼92a RNA已知结构模型具有较强一致性(evidence: figure-0)。
Fig. 2图注描述了用于解析异质结构的聚类方法:将每条读段的结构谱编码为向量,碱基分为0(匹配碱基)、1(修饰碱基)、2(误判碱基),并填充至参考RNA长度L;随后对赖氨酸核糖开关化学处理样本的向量化结构谱进行UMAP降维,按DeCoRE识别的簇着色,并用轮廓系数评估聚类质量(evidence: figure-1)。
Fig. 2图注还显示DeCoRE在赖氨酸核糖开关中识别出两个结构簇,并在包含抗终止子与转录终止子两种互斥构象的区域展示其反应性评分,三个关键区分区域被高亮标注(evidence: figure-1)。
Fig. 3图注描述了在体外生成枯草芽孢杆菌16S rRNA转录中间体并用纳米孔DRS结构探测方法检测其结构的实验流程,并展示各中间体与全长16S rRNA在共享核苷酸区域反应性评分的PCC,以及136个中间体的反应性评分热图(按3′端比对位置以10-nt分辨率分类)(evidence: figure-2)。
Fig. 4图注描述了五个高覆盖度16S rRNA转录中间体化学处理样本读段向量化结构谱的UMAP,以及1–270 nt、1–320 nt、1–670 nt区域各构象反应性评分的PCA散点图,点大小反映构象在相应转录中间体中的相对丰度(evidence: figure-3)。
提供的脚本静态观察记录包含固定提交894bd3d6d71671d39b9c6a5a252598b6a1da6a17下的若干文件路径与SHA256,其中dataprocessing.py的静态观察显示以分块方式读取事件文件(chunksize=50000)(evidence: script-0, script-1, script-2, script-3)。

ai.title_zh: 面向抽象与推理语料库的向量符号代数方法
ai.summary_zh: 该论文提出一种受认知科学启发的 ARC-AGI 求解器,将 System 1 直觉与 System 2 推理结合,采用基于向量符号代数(VSA)的神经符号方法,通过以对象为中心的程序合成来表征抽象对象、引导解搜索并支持样本高效的神经学习。摘要报告了初步结果:ARC-AGI-1-Train 得分 10.8%、ARC-AGI-1-Eval 得分 3.0%,Sort-of-ARC 得分 94.5%、1D-ARC 得分 83.1%,并称后者以极小计算成本超过 GPT-4。论文发表于 Npj unconventional computing(2026-10-01),DOI 为 10.1038/s44335-026-00100-5,作者代码位于 https://github.com/ijoffe/ARC-VSA-2025。提供的证据还包含四张 ARC-AGI 任务图注(0962bcdd、54d9e175、a61f2674、a61ba2ce)以及若干源码文件的静态观察记录。
learning_points: 论文将 ARC-AGI 定位为生成式、少样本的流体智力基准,并指出其对当前最先进 AI 系统仍极难。
求解器采用神经符号方法,基于向量符号代数(VSA),并整合 System 1 直觉与 System 2 推理,强调高效与可解释。
核心机制是以对象为中心的程序合成,用 VSA 表征抽象对象、引导解搜索并支持样本高效的神经学习。
摘要报告初步结果:ARC-AGI-1-Train 10.8%、ARC-AGI-1-Eval 3.0%、Sort-of-ARC 94.5%、1D-ARC 83.1%。
论文称 1D-ARC 结果以极小计算成本超过 GPT-4,并认为自己是首个将 VSA 应用于 ARC-AGI 的工作。
证据中的图注展示了四类 ARC-AGI 任务模式:多色对象变换为特定更大对象、按中心像素颜色为灰色像素分隔的黑色区域着色、将最短条纹重着色为红、最高条纹为蓝、把四个块重排为小网格上的空心方框。
提供的源码静态观察涉及 src/grid.py、src/object.py、src/objobj_solver.py、src/perception.py,固定提交为 c031a9c6b4885ab03b28fbfdcd97b6b3693df564。
作者代码未被执行,静态检查不构成复现验证,因此上述性能数字与实现细节均未在本证据范围内得到独立验证。
limitations: 作者代码未运行,静态检查不是复现验证,不能宣称已复现或结果一致。
摘要中的性能数字(10.8%、3.0%、94.5%、83.1%)为论文自报的初步结果,未在本证据范围内独立验证。
证据未明示输入尺度、图号与具体数据结构的对应关系,相关细节保持未知。
证据未提供各源码文件的具体静态观察内容,仅给出路径、提交与哈希,无法据此推断实现逻辑。
证据未说明 VSA 的具体编码方式、维度或超参数,也未说明 System 1/System 2 的具体交互机制。
证据未提供与 GPT-4 对比的计算成本量化数据,无法核实“极小计算成本”的说法。
证据未提供数据集划分、评测协议或统计显著性信息。
证据未提供许可、期刊指标或同行评审状态等信息。
证据未说明四张图注与求解器内部模块的对应关系。
证据未说明代码仓库的可用性、依赖或运行环境。
作者代码未运行；静态检查不等于图形复现或结果验证。

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: Development of the MCCv platform.a, Schematic of the MCCv platform including: nanoscale chromatin structure, the regulatory landscape of the locus and phasing of other alleles in the locus. b, Schematic of the MCCv method. Oligonucleotide probes are designed over the variant of interest in heterozygous cells. Ultra-short-range ligation junctions (<800 bp) define the nanoscale topology at the variant. Long-range junctions (1 kb to 1 Mb) define the locus structure. c, Metaplots of MCCv nanoscale chromatin architecture heatmaps for inactive (reference) and active (alternate) alleles from 41 gain-of-function enhancer variants (Jurkat cells, six replicates, 1-bp bin size). The matrix represents the contact frequency between short-range ligation junctions (<800 bp) to visualize nanoscale chromatin architecture from single alleles. Below is a kernel density estimate (KDE) plot of genomic distances between two basepairs that make up the ultra-short-range ligation junctions for both reference and alternate alleles. d, Individual 2D nanoscale chromatin architecture heatmap for reference (left) and alternate (right) alleles of rs2793109 (1-bp bin size, n = 6, merged β = 0.75). The schematic is for nucleosome sliding with a fixed internucleosomal distance in the inactive alleles. At the nucleosome-depleted region, contacts between potential transcription factors in the alternate allele may lead to regions of high signal adjacent to transcription factor-binding sites. The underlying RUNX family motif is shown with the effect of the rs2793109 alternate allele highlighted. e, MCCv from rs2793109. A difference plot (reference minus alternate), DNase I sequencing and CTCF ChIP–seq are shown underneath. f, Using MCCv to phase other heterozygous variants within a locus. g, TT-seq skew from MCCv-phased variants in introns of ZNF438 (n = 13) and ZEB1 (n = 15) (mean ± s.e.m., Wilcoxon’s signed-rank test, paired, two-sided, two-stage step-up procedure for multiple-test correction: ZNF438 q = 0.435; ZEB1 q = 0.0002). NS, not significant; oligo, oligonucleotide.Source data

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption: Linking GWAS variants to genes using MCC.a, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) of scATAC–seq from peripheral blood, colored by enrichment of lead SNPs in open chromatin peaks per cluster54. b, Clustered hierarchical heatmap for haplotypes with at least one molecular mechanism assigned. Mechanistic assignment weight = 1/(number of distinct candidate mechanisms among SNPs in the haplotype). c, Micro-C from CD4+ T cells (3-kb bin size; pooled from three replicates), ATAC–seq (CD4+, unstimulated blue, stimulated red, overlay) and CTCF ChIP–seq for the 1q24.3–25.1 locus: MCC for rs75084219 (eczema), rs78037933 (vitiligo), rs1474379684 (celiac disease) and rs62803660 (Crohn’s disease) with SNP–promoter contacts highlighted in gray (3 biological replicates, each with 6 technical replicates (18 in total)). d, Comparison of the number of variant–promoter ligation junctions identified by MCC (median = 828.2) and Micro-C (median = 2.07) (n = 349 promoter contacts measured across 2 independent libraries for both methods, median (center line), 25th and 75th percentiles (box limits) and whiskers extending to the most extreme values within 1.5× the interquartile range). e, Gene ontology overrepresentation analysis of MCC-prioritized genes in CD4+ T cells (top ten pathways by gene ratio are shown (total significant hits = 251)). The gene ratio is defined as the number of genes in the input list that are annotated to the corresponding term (function) over the number of genes in the input list. f, Comparison between the enrichment of genes with the highest number of MCC contacts (primary nominated gene) versus genes with the second highest number of MCC contacts (secondary nominated gene) compared to background (all genes ±1 Mb from captured variants). For reference, the enrichment scores of the nearest and second nearest genes for each variant are also shown (essentiality (Depmap), drug target and approved drugs (open targets) and primary immunodeficiency (Genomics England)) (χ2 test, two-sided P values reported in Source data). cDCs, conventional dendritic cells; MAIT, mucosal-associated invariant T cells; NK, natural killer cells; pDCs, plasmacytoid dendritic cells; TCM, central memory T cells; TEM, effector memory T cells; Treg, regulatory T cells; B int, intermediate B cells.Source data

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.caption: MCCv identifies GWAS variants that alter chromatin architecture.a, Alternate or reference normalized junction counts at MCCv peaks for heterozygous SNPs (n depends on how many donors are heterozygous for the SNP from which the peak is derived (minimum of six independent libraries per donor), paired, two-sided Student’s t-test, local false discovery rate (FDR) estimation). b, Clustered hierarchical heatmap of the average ratio of alternate to reference junction counts for peaks overlapping different regulatory element categories per SNP. c, Percentage of variants with significant MCCv changes (two-sided χ2 test, disease variants n = 227). Enrichment over controls (enrichment, P, n control): cell type = IMID variants intersecting monocyte enhancers (7.5, 0.0015 and 14); haplotype = SNPs in haplotype that do not intersect CD4+ T cell enhancers (7.5, 2.73 × 10−13 and 82); enhancer = variants that intersect CD4+ T cell enhancers but are not associated with IMIDs (2.2, 0.000014 and 76). d, MCCv from rs10950648 with SNP–promoter contact in gray. Difference plots (alternate minus reference), ATAC–seq (CD4+, unstimulated blue, stimulated red) and CTCF ChIP–seq shown underneath. e, Nanoscale contact maps of rs10950648 with 10-bp directional windowing. They are mirrored on the diagonal. PRDM1 motif and enhancer sequences are shown with the effect of the alternate allele highlighted (n = 12, merged β = -1.09). f, ATAC–seq read skew for rs10950648 (q = 0.024) and rs9526002 (q = 0.025) (n = 2 donors, mean ± s.d.). g, Allelic expression of primary or secondary nominated genes phased to a heterozygous variant: 88 variants (102 variant–gene pairs) tested. Twenty-three genes showed donor-level skew (variable-phased SNPs (n) per gene; two-sided, Wilcoxon’s signed-rank test was used per donor (Fisher’s method across donors) with the Benjamini–Hochberg correction). h, Percentage of allelically imbalanced genes by SNP–gene categories. Backgrounds were genome-wide allelic gene imbalance, 10.0% (231 out of 2,313) and allelic gene imbalance without MCCv skew, 8.9% (17 out of 190). The percentage of genes showing allelic imbalance linked to variants with evidence of MCCv changes (category: n variant-–gene pairs, enrichment over genome-wide (p), enrichment over MCCv (p); secondary genes: 6 of 23, 2.61 (0.0316); primary genes 10 of 33, 3.03 (0.0316), 3.40 (0.038); primary or secondary: 16 of 45, 3.55 (0.0001), 3.99 (0.0002) (two-tailed χ2 test).Source data

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.caption: rs4409785 acts through a gain-of-function CTCF site.a, Associations of rs4409785 from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) GWAS catalog, with −log10(P) versus log10(odds ratio) for the tested allele plotted as a volcano. Associations reported with reference T allele are shown in purple, whereas associations reported with the alternate C allele are shown in green. Representative autoimmune disease signals are labeled (autoimmune thyroid disease (ATD), RA, MS, myasthenia gravis (MG) and vitiligo). b, CTCF consensus motif and the sequence around rs4409785 in humans. The effect of rs4409785 is highlighted in gray. Sequence alignment from early hominins and chimps is shown below. c, MCCv basepair resolution footprinting for reference and alternate alleles with the rs4409785 location marked by a red triangle. Corresponding nanoscale heatmaps are shown as in Fig. 1d (bin size = 1 bp, 800-bp window, n = 6 merged per allele and merged β = 1.09). d, CTCF ChIP–seq (q = 0.000123), ATAC–seq (q = 0.000123) and H3K27ac ChIP–seq (q = 0.156) skew in heterozygous donors (n = 15 CTCF or ATAC, n = 12 H3K27ac; two-sided Wilcoxon’s matched-pairs, signed-rank test, two-stage step-up procedure for multiple-test correction, mean ± s.d.). e, CTCF ChIP–seq and ATAC–seq reads per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads-normalized signal from three donors who are either homozygous reference (purple) or alternate (green) for rs4409785. f, MCCv profiles for rs4409785 alleles with corresponding ATAC (CD4+, unstimulated blue, stimulated red, overlay) and a unified CTCF track. Capture probe location or SNP is marked by the red triangle and CTCF elements with orientation are marked by purple triangles.Source data

figures.label: Fig. 5
figures.caption: Direct read-out of genome editing with MCCv.a, Schematic illustrating coupling of basepair-level editing technologies with basepair resolution MCCv. Incomplete genome editing is leveraged to make a population of cells with mixed alleles become deconvoluted with the platform’s single-allele capabilities. b, Base editing experimental design with CTCF guide RNA sequence as well as locations of rs4409785 and the CTCF motif shown. The location of an upstream control guide outside the extended CTCF motif but within the MCC capture oligonucleotide is also shown. c, Experimental set-up of the CTCF and control edits in primary T cells. Edits were performed in parallel and mixed to avoid double editing. The cell mix was then fixed and captured by MCCv. As these cells were heterozygous for risk variant rs4409785 this led to six different editing outcomes that were deconvoluted by single-allele MCCv. To increase the depth of the data, six independent replicates were performed. d, Allele-specific (relative to rs4409785) editing efficiency of BE4max in primary CD4+ T cell for both control and CTCF guides. Editing efficiencies are shown as a percentage of NGS reads with C-to-T substitution. Where multiple Cs could be edited, the one with highest editing efficiency is shown (n = 2 independent experiments, mean ± s.d.). e, Edit-MCCv tracks for reference (purple) and alternate (green) alleles of rs4409785 with wild-type, control edit and CTCF edit shown. A CTCF ChIP–seq track is shown underneath. f, Nanoscale heatmaps for rs4409785 reference and alternate alleles with corresponding edit type (bin size = 1 bp, 800-bp window, n = 6 merged per allele). NGS, next-generation sequencing.Source data

figures.label: Fig. 6
figures.caption: Neo-CTCF site blocks super-enhancer–promoter interactions, reducing SESN3 expression.a, A 2.5-kb, binned Micro-C, ATAC–seq (CD4+, unstimulated blue, stimulated red, overlay) and CTCF ChIP–seq for the 11q21 locus. Bulk MCCs from the promoters of SESN3 and FAM76B are shown in blue. The location of the super-enhancer is highlighted in gray. b, Phased enhancer–promoter contacts (SESN3 (q = 0.018, n = 24 peaks across six independent MCC libraries) and FAM76B (q = 0.916, n = 24 peaks across six independent MCC libraries), Student’s t-test, two-stage step-up procedure for multiple-test correction, mean ± s.e.m.) and intron-rich RNA (SESN3 (q = 0.00054, n = 37 phased heterozygous variants across two donors) and FAM76B (q = 0.11, n = 45 phased heterozygous variants across two donors), Wilcoxon’s signed-rank test, two-stage step-up procedure for multiple-test correction, mean ± s.e.m.) from MCCv-phased heterozygous variants for both SESN3 and FAM76B. c, Working mechanistic model for the 11q21 risk locus. The neo-CTCF site competes with canonical upstream boundary elements for convergent downstream CTCF sites, forming a subdomain that isolates the super-enhancer away from the promoter of SESN3.Source data

figures.label: Fig. 7
figures.caption: Functional characterization of SESN3.a, Experimental design of the mouse EAE model. b, Clinical EAE score for both Rosa26 and Sesn3 cohorts. For each day where both cohorts were represented, scores were compared statistically (n = 6 mice per condition, day 12, q = 0.0024; day 13, q = 0.0089; day 14, q = 0.0024; two-sided, unpaired, Student’s t-test with single pooled variance, mean ± s.e.m.). c, Dot plot representation of SESN gene family members’ scRNA-seq expression from synovial tissue of patients wth RA56. d, Representative flow cytometry contour plots showing a positive population of CD4+ (y axis) and phospho-4E-BP1+ (mTORC1 signaling marker, x axis). e, Western blots for FLAG-tagged SESN3 or GATOR2 complex subunit, WDR59, either from cell lysate (input) or from co-immunoprecipitation using anti-FLAG antibody-conjugated beads. Experimental conditions compared were a medium control (fed state) versus a starved state in Hanks’ balanced salt solution (HBSS) with or without various free amino acids. Specific indicated free amino acids were added to the starved state during the 1-h starvation at 500 µM. f, Schematic for working model of the effect of rs4409785 on reducing SESN3 gene expression and, in turn, how this may affect mTORC1 signaling in starvation conditions, specifically low tryptophan availability. AAVS1, adeno-associated virus integration site 1; CNS, central nervous system; E-P, enhancer–promoter; GAPDH, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase; IFN, interferon; IP, immunoprecipitation; MOG, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein; MThi, mitochondrial high; mTORC1, mTOR complex 1; PTX, pertussis toxin.Source data

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 1
figures.caption: Optimisation and validation of MCCv at gain-of-function enhancers.a, Schematic overview of the MCCv bioinformatics suite. b, Skew data for ATAC and H3K27ac ChIP sequencing at the selected 42 enhancer elements demonstrating potential gain-of-function activity at the enhancer (n = 42 variants, read counts averaged across 3 independent donors, per variant reference vs. alternate comparison – Wilcoxon sign-rank test, two-sided, two-stage step-up procedure for multiple test correction, q < 0.000001 (ATAC) and q = 0.000029 (H3K27ac)). c, Quantification of allelic dropout post MCCv single-allele analysis. figures.caption: MCCv at an oncogenic super-enhancer.a, Quantification of ATAC and RUNX1 ChIP-seq skew at rs2793109 (mean ± s.e.m., paired Student’s t-test, two-sided, two-stage step-up procedure for multiple test correction; ATAC – n = 3 biological replicates, q = 0.039; RUNX1 ChIP-seq – n = 4 biological replicates, q = 0.030). b, Quantification of MCCv junction count differences between reference and alternate alleles at MCCv peaks for the rs2793109 variant. figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 3
figures.caption: MCC can interpret previously intractable loci.a, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) of single-cell ATAC sequencing from peripheral blood. b, Upset plot of SNP prioritisation pipeline output. A total of 3238 IMID-GWAS signals were analysed, with 1441 having at least 1 SNP being identified in the six molecular mechanisms tested (coding, splicing, enhancer, CTCF, promoter, UTR). A total of 727 were classified as CTCF altering or enhancer altering in activated CD4+/CD8+ T cells or Monocytes. c, Enrichment scores of IMID-associated SNPs for each molecular mechanism tested in the SNP prioritisation pipeline (n = 124,000) compared to dbSNP151 common variants across the genome (n = 15,000,000). Enrichment scores were calculated as: the fraction of GWAS variants that can be explained by the tested molecular mechanisms over fraction of total common variants explained by the tested molecular mechanism (Χ2 test, two-sided, 3’UTR (P = 0.001), coding (P = 0.145), CTCF (P = 0.203), promoter (P = 3.68 × 10−10), splicing (P = 7.97 × 10−13, enhancer (4.67 × 10−53)). d, 3 kb binned Micro-C, ATAC (CD4+, unstimulated blue, stimulated red, overlay) and CTCF ChIP-seq for the 10q21.3 locus with MCC from rs12766391. e, 1.5 kb binned Micro-C, ATAC (CD4+, unstimulated blue, stimulated red, overlay) and CTCF ChIP-seq for the RUNX3 locus with MCC from rs57974094 (green) and rs4265380 (blue). cDCs, conventional dendritic cells; MAIT, mucosal-associated invariant T cells; NK, natural killer cells; pDCs, plasmacytoid dendritic cells; Tcm, central memory T cells; Tem, effector memory T cells; Treg, regulatory T cells; B int, intermediate B cells. figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 4
figures.caption: Further characterisation of MCC derived regulatory contacts at GWAS loci.a, Quantification of normalized MCC junctions at the genes in the multi-trait locus for all variants shown in Fig. 2c (n = 18 (3 donors, with 6 independent MCC libraries each), mean ± s.d., paired Student’s t-test, two-sided, two-stage step-up method for multiple test correction, P values reported in source data). b, Enrichment of variant–promoter ligation junctions compared to background between Micro-C (median = 1.33) and MCC (median = 5.5). Calculated using variant–promoter contacts in Fig. 2d divided by the mean junction counts at random locations that did not overlap peaks within the bounds of the two most extreme MCC peaks either side of the capture oligo (n = 349 promoters contacts measured across 2 independent libraries for both methods, median (centre line), 25th and 75th percentiles (box limits), and whiskers extending to the most extreme values within 1.5 × the interquartile range). c, Schematic of LotronMCC peak calling including how it assigns peaks and classifies them into regulatory element categories. For each viewpoint, 27 individual signal thresholds are computed comprised of the rolling mean coverage of MCC signal or background (with varying windows), or the fold increase of signal over background (with varying thresholds). A peak is called if a region exceeds 10 out of 27 signal thresholds. Peaks are assigned as promoters based on open chromatin and transcription start site intersection. CTCF peaks are assigned on open chromatin and CTCF ChIP-seq intersection. Remaining open chromatin intersections are assigned as enhancers. d, 2D KDE plot of average Lotron MCC peak score for different regulatory element types (promoter in green, enhancer in blue, and CTCF in purple) per SNP versus the corresponding number of those element types forming MCC peaks with that SNP. e, KDE plot showing the distance between the MCC prioritised promoter and corresponding SNP (median = 32 kb) compared to the nearest promoter to that SNP (median = 17 kb). Source data

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 5
figures.caption: MCCv identifies regions of 3D genome skew in primary cells.a, Count data for PCR deduplicated reads containing the target SNP for a subset (donor 1 only) of heterozygous SNPs (n = 147 variant read counts from 6 independent MCC libraries from a single donor). This data is used to variant call the genotype of captured GWAS sites before applying the MCCv single-allele analysis pipeline. b, Summary of the number of variants captured by MCC (total) and those amenable to allelic analysis (heterozygous). c, Visualisation of the total number of heterozygous variants and the breakdown of those where allelic data was successfully generated using MCCv. We also include a theoretical estimation of the number of variants that could generate allele-specific data in a dpnII-based 3 C experiment (for example Capture C), where variants had to fall within 60 bp of a dpnII-cut site to be classified as successful. d, The distribution of SNPs in the MCCv dataset in terms of percentage of peaks which are significantly altered between alleles (relative to the total number of MCCv peak for that SNP). e, as in Fig. 3a but data has been filtered for promoters, CTCF, or enhancer elements before plotting. f, MCCv profile for rs9526002, with SNP-promoter contact highlighted in grey. Difference plots show alternate-minus-reference contacts, with CD4+ ATAC-seq and CTCF ChIP-seq tracks below. g, rs10950648 nanoscale contact maps generated using 10-bp directional windowing and mirrored on the diagonal. The AP-1 motif and enhancer sequence are shown, with the effect of the alternate allele highlighted (n = 12 (2 donors, 6 independent MCC libraries each), merged β = −1.10). Source data

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 6
figures.caption: Further visualisation of nanoscale chromatin architecture at disease-associated enhancers.a, Schematic of converting nanoscale heatmaps into directionally windowed heatmaps for the visualisation of contacts between transcription factor motifs. Reads that give rise to ligation junctions are thought to be protected from MNase cutting by bound transcription factors. The direction of the extension of the reads can be leveraged to estimate the position of the putatively bound transcription factor. This converts the negative signal of the transcription factor footprint into positive signal equating to potential contacts between transcription factors. b, MCC ultra tile over the rs10950648-containing enhancer (n = 6 independent MCC libraries, bin size = 2, tile = 2.2 kb). Corresponding ATAC (CD4+, unstimulated blue, stimulated red, overlay) and a unified CTCF track are shown underneath. The capture probe/SNP locations are shown by the horizontal bar and red triangle respectively. Zoom in shows MCCv single-allele directional windowed heatmaps for reference and alternate alleles at the variant shown in Fig. 3e. c, As in b for the rs9526002-containing enhancer with zoom in corresponding to directional windowed heatmap as shown in Extended Data Fig. 5g (n = 6 independent MCC libraries, bin size = 2, tile = 1.9 kb). d and e, Footprinting data from ATAC-seq combined with MCCv based capture enrichment (above) and 1D-MCCv footprinting (below) for both reference and alternate alleles of rs10950648 and rs9526002. SNP position is indicated with the red triangle.
figures.attribution: Joseph C. Hamley; Weijiao Zhang; Daniel Willmott; Lucia Y. Chen; Vassilena Sharlandjieva; Hangpeng Li; et al.. Single-allele nanoscale mapping of regulatory variants.. DOI: 10.1038/s41588-026-02776-8. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Extended Data Fig. 7
figures.caption: Quantifying the impact of disease-associated variants on nanoscale chromatin architecture.a, Effect size estimate of GLM from basepairC at tested SNPs (n = 231) (bottom 20% of variants based on read counts were filtered). Estimates were done between maps of different genotypes (allele-specific) (Genotype, mean β-coefficient (effect size) = 0.293). Random combinations of 6 reference and 6 alternate allele sample matrices were compared (mean β-coefficient = 0.097) (median (centre line), 25th and 75th percentiles (box limits), and whiskers extending to most extreme values within 1.5 × interquartile range). b, Effect size from basepairC matrix difference modelling in Jurkat controls (prioritised using ATAC skew) vs. T cell disease associated enhancers (prioritised by ATAC intersection only). Variants within lowest 10% of read counts for MCCv nanoscale maps were filtered from the correlation. Gain-of-function (MCCv nanoscale effect size ≥ 0.2) and loss-of-function (MCCv nanoscale effect size ≤ -0.2) variants are highlighted in green and purple respectively. Variants highlighted throughout the study are indicated on the plot (Jurkat controls – n = 38 variants (6 independent MCC libraries), IMID variants – n = 191 variants (6 independent MCC libraries from 1-3 biological donors, median (centre line), 25th and 75th percentiles (box limits), and whiskers extending to the most extreme values within 1.5 × the interquartile range.). c, Allelic ratio from ATAC-seq versus effect size from basepairC matrix difference modelling (n = 201, two-sided Spearman’s ρ = 0.62, P = 2.2 × 10−16). Variants within the lowest 10% of read counts for either ATAC or MCCv were filtered from the correlation. Nominally gain-of-function (ATAC allelic ratio ≥ 0.55 & MCCv nanoscale effect size ≥ 0.05) and loss-of-function (ATAC allelic ratio ≤ 0.45 & MCCv nanoscale effect size ≤ -0.05) variants are highlighted in green and purple respectively. figures.caption: 11q21 contains a pleiotropic autoimmune risk locus within a gene desert.a, Percentage MCCv skew (percentage of total peaks demonstrating skew) versus number of NCBI GWAS catalogue associations for all MCCv SNPs in dataset, with rs4409785 highlighted in red. b, Associations between rs4409785 and various immune-related traits in the All of Us database. Only hits with a significant FDR corrected P value are displayed (n cases/controls = 257/98802 (SIRS), 377 /98552 (Celiac), 1311/95544 (Alopecia), 436/83656 (Preeclampsia), 254/99186 (Narcolepsy), 4683/164303 (Sepsis), 4108/163806 (HPV), 260/98019 (Streptococcus infection), odds ratio ± standard error, Firth logistic regression, two-sided; Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction) (SIRS = serious inflammatory response syndrome, HPV = Human papillomavirus). c, DeepHeam absolute damage score for each classifier grouped into molecular categories. Damage score calculated as the difference between reference and alternate allele predictions for tested epigenetic classifier. d, Locus zoom plot for the association of rs4409785 with rheumatoid arthritis. R2 values for nearby SNPs are displayed from high-linkage (red) to low-linkage (blue). The molecular effect of this variant is shown underneath by genomic tracks of CTCF ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and H3K27ac ChIP-seq from donors homozygous for either the reference (purple) or alternate risk (green) allele. e, KDE plot of primary genomic distance between two base-pairs which make up ultra-short ligation junctions ( < 800 bp) for rs4409785. f, Absolute log2 fold change of junction counts between reference and alternate alleles at called Lotron MCC peak for rs4409785 (n = 6, paired Student’s t-test, two-sided, local FDR estimate with fdrtools). Key CTCF peaks as well as the peaks belonging to the SESN3 super-enhancer are highlighted as being significant. Source data
